title: Server Software Component: Transport Agent
summary: Transport Agent persistence targets Microsoft Exchange mail flow. Exchange lets developers write compiled transport agents that the server invokes at defined stages of the transport pipeline, the code path every message follows on its way to a mailbox. Legitimate agents perform filtering, journaling, attachment handling, or signature stamping. A malicious agent is registered the same way, so it loads with the transport service, runs in the same trusted context, and inspects or rewrites messages without breaking mail delivery. Because the agent sees every message, the adversary can select narrowly: copy attachments for a named recipient, capture messages that match a subject pattern, or alter content before delivery, and the mailbox side of the exchange looks entirely normal. Persistence comes from server-side registration and compiled files rather than from anything inside a mailbox, so mailbox audit logs alone will not show it. Detection needs to compare the registered agent list and the transport agent directories against a known baseline, review the Exchange setup and configuration logs generated when agents are registered, and follow the account that performed the change. Legitimate agent changes are rare, documented, and usually installed together with software updates.

beginner.definition: A transport agent is a small program that Microsoft Exchange runs on every email as it passes through the mail server. Companies use these programs to filter spam, add signatures or keep copies of messages. This technique is about an attacker registering their own agent so the mail server runs hidden code on every message.
beginner.whyItMatters: Mail servers carry contracts, invoices, password resets and private conversations, so an attacker inside mail flow can read far more than one mailbox. Because the agent is part of the mail server itself, there is no visible rule in the mailbox of the victim and no message in the sent folder. It can also copy files quietly for later theft, which is hard to spot in normal mail logs. Only a review of the programs registered on the server reveals it.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains administrator rights on the Exchange server, often through stolen credentials.
They write a compiled program that fits the agent interface of the mail server and place it on the server.
They register the program with Exchange so it is called during a chosen stage of mail processing.
The server loads the agent with the transport service, keeping normal mail delivery working.
The agent reads each message and acts only on messages that match the rules of the attacker.
Registered code is stored on the server, so the agent returns after restarts and updates.
beginner.example: Think of a large post office where every letter passes a sorting desk. A real clerk checks addresses and stamps parcels. If somebody secretly hires a new clerk who only copies the contents of letters addressed to one company, the post still arrives on time and the original sorting staff notice nothing unusual.
takeaways: Mail flow code is a hidden place to live, because it leaves no trace in the mailbox of a user.
Keep a baseline of registered transport agents and the files that support them.
Review Exchange configuration logs and the account that registered each agent.

objectives: Explain what an Exchange transport agent does during normal mail processing.
Describe how a malicious agent is registered and kept loaded across restarts.
Identify the server-side artefacts that reveal an unauthorised transport agent.
Distinguish an approved mail flow program from an attacker registered one.
Plan a review of registered agents as part of mail server hardening.
